metadata.narrative: Pretend that you are a senior research fellow at a national public health institute and create a comprehensive research report about the health benefits of outdoor exposure and Vitamin D today. In the report explain to the regular public recent research from peer reviewed journals to provide a clear, actionable overview of the topic. Provide a high level overview of the report's key findings (and recommendations), explain any interconnected relationship, clearly differentiate between the physiological benefits derived specifically from Vitamin D and the independent benefits derived from being outdoors, provide a detailed analysis of the benefits and specific health considerations for different demographics (different ages, different sex), and for each group, cite at least one unique benefit or risk. Also include quantifiable recommendations. Detail the recommended duration of sun exposure, accounting for different variables. Provide the consensus daily supplemental intake recommendations in IU and clearly differentiate between Vitamin D2 and Vitamin D3. Finally summarize the primary health risks associated with both underexposure and overexposure of sun/vitamin D. Mention some mitigation strategies to avoid both.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): continuous single-agent full-text search with sparse committed context and line-per-sentence cited prose answers parsed into the organizer schema.

answer.text: As a senior research fellow at a national public health institute, I want to give the public a clear, actionable picture of what recent peer-reviewed science says about sunlight, outdoor time, and vitamin D.
The core finding is that sunlight-driven vitamin D synthesis and simply spending time outdoors deliver overlapping but distinct benefits, so both matter rather than either alone.

Our headline recommendations are brief, regular sun exposure tailored to skin tone and season, a vitamin D3 supplement in the 600-2,000 IU daily range depending on age and risk, and balancing sun exposure against skin cancer risk through shade, clothing, and timing rather than total avoidance.

Vitamin D3 is made when UVB rays convert a skin precursor into previtamin D3, which the liver and kidneys activate into the hormone governing calcium absorption, bone mineralization, and immune regulation, and this sun-made form remains active in the bloodstream roughly twice as long as vitamin D from diet or pills, so exposure and pills are not interchangeable even though both raise the same blood marker, 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Independent of vitamin D itself, being outdoors lowers cortisol, reduces blood pressure, improves mood, and increases physical activity, effects that persist even when vitamin D status is unchanged.

One analysis found roughly 30 minutes outdoors was linked to about a 7 percent lower depression risk and a 9 percent lower risk of high blood pressure, benefits tied to light, greenery, and movement rather than vitamin D synthesis.
Outdoor light also helps regulate the circadian rhythm and boosts alertness through pathways separate from UVB-driven vitamin D production.
Health considerations differ meaningfully across age and sex, and each group carries at least one distinct benefit or risk.
Infants are uniquely vulnerable because their vitamin D stores at birth last only about a month and breast milk contains little vitamin D, so maternal deficiency directly compounds a newborn's risk.
A baby is typically born with only about 75 percent of its mother's vitamin D level, making prenatal sufficiency a distinct priority for pregnant women.

Children and adolescents uniquely benefit from building peak bone mass, since roughly a quarter of adult bone mass accrues during just two pubertal years, while outdoor time separately improves focus in children with ADHD.
Adult men show a distinct hormonal benefit: supplementing 3,332 IU of vitamin D daily for a year raised free testosterone by roughly 20 percent in one study.

Adult women carry a unique skeletal risk, since one in three women over 50 will suffer an osteoporotic fracture compared with one in five men, a gap driven largely by accelerated post-menopausal bone loss.

Older adults face the clearest fall-and-fracture risk: supplementing 700-1,000 IU of vitamin D3 daily reduced falls by 19 to 26 percent, and doses above 800 IU with calcium cut fracture risk by 10 to 15 percent.

Older adults also gain a distinct immune benefit, since low vitamin D has been linked to a 64 percent higher risk of community-acquired pneumonia, prompting Irish researchers to recommend supplementation specifically for adults over 50.
Recommended sun exposure duration depends heavily on skin pigmentation, season, latitude, and time of day.

A light-skinned person at midday in summer typically needs only about 10 minutes of exposure on roughly 10 percent of body surface area, while darker, more melanin-rich skin needs two to three times longer for the same vitamin D yield.
In winter that same light-skinned person may need 30 minutes and a darker-skinned person up to 90 minutes, because a lower sun angle reduces UVB penetration.

A satellite-modeling study across Indian cities found clear-sky exposure for 1,000 IU ranged from about 11 to 22 minutes at midday but climbed to 85-133 minutes in northern latitudes during winter and monsoon season once cloud cover was included.

The optimal window for cutaneous vitamin D production is roughly 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., exposure should stop at about one-third of the dose that would produce faint skin redness, and unprotected exposure should be avoided whenever the UV Index reaches 3 or above.

On supplementation, two consensus bodies offer complementary daily intake targets in International Units: the Institute of Medicine recommends 600 IU for ages 1-70 and 800 IU for those 71 and older, while the Endocrine Society, focused on people at risk of deficiency, suggests higher ranges of 600-1,000 IU for children and 1,500-2,000 IU for adults.
Tolerable upper limits also rise with age, from about 1,000 IU for young infants up to 4,000 IU for most adults, including pregnant and lactating women.

Vitamin D comes in two supplemental forms, plant-derived D2 (ergocalciferol) and animal-derived D3 (cholecalciferol, the form skin naturally makes), and D3 is considered clearly superior, raising and sustaining blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels roughly 87 percent more effectively than D2.

A controlled fortification trial found D3 raised serum vitamin D by about 75 percent over 12 weeks compared with only 33-34 percent for D2 at the same 600 IU dose, which is why clinicians now favor D3 specifically.

Underexposure carries well-documented risks, including rickets in children, osteomalacia and osteoporosis in adults, muscle weakness, higher fall and fracture rates in older adults, and greater susceptibility to respiratory infections.

Overexposure carries a different risk profile: UV radiation is a proven carcinogen responsible for roughly one million skin cancers and about 8,000 melanoma deaths annually in the United States, alongside accelerated skin aging.

True oral vitamin D toxicity is rare, generally requiring roughly 50,000 IU per day for months before hypercalcemia symptoms such as nausea, weakness, and kidney strain appear, and toxicity cannot occur from sun exposure alone because skin self-regulates production.

Sensible mitigation bridges both risks: seek brief, unprotected midday exposure for vitamin D synthesis, then use broad-spectrum SPF 30-plus sunscreen, protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, and shade once approaching your skin's burn threshold.
People with photosensitizing conditions such as lupus, or on certain sun-sensitizing medications, may need stricter shade-and-clothing-first strategies instead of deliberate sun exposure.
Checking the daily UV Index and periodically testing blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D remain the simplest ways to stay in the safe middle ground between deficiency and overexposure.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- Aim for about 950 words, excluding citation markers. 1024 words is a hard
  limit set by the evaluation, and an over-length report costs a full rewrite,
  so plan the report's scope to land under the target rather than writing long
  and trimming.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

query.description: A natural-language query for evidence relevant to the research request.

k.description: Number of fused passages to return (default 10).

budget_tokens_per_result.description: Maximum approximate tokens staged per result. Text is bounded at tokens × 5 characters and cut at the final line break before that boundary. Default 4096.

tools.name: commit_context

documents.description: Evidence-worthy staged documents to retain. An empty array explicitly rejects the whole staged batch.

reason.description: The distinct evidence, claim, perspective, date, name, counter-evidence, or coverage area this document uniquely contributes.

The core finding is that sunlight-driven vitamin D synthesis and simply spending time outdoors deliver overlapping but distinct benefits, so both matter rather than either alone.

Our headline recommendations are brief, regular sun exposure tailored to skin tone and season, a vitamin D3 supplement in the 600-2,000 IU daily range depending on age and risk, and balancing sun exposure against skin cancer risk through shade, clothing, and timing rather than total avoidance.

Vitamin D3 is made when UVB rays convert a skin precursor into previtamin D3, which the liver and kidneys activate into the hormone governing calcium absorption, bone mineralization, and immune regulation, and this sun-made form appears to remain active in the bloodstream roughly twice as long as vitamin D from diet or pills, so sun exposure and pills are not interchangeable even though both raise the same blood marker, 25-hydroxyvitamin D. [shard_02457_77621]
Independent of vitamin D itself, being outdoors lowers cortisol, reduces blood pressure, improves mood, and increases physical activity, effects that persist even when vitamin D status is unchanged. [shard_03248_69687]
One analysis found roughly 30 minutes outdoors was linked to about a 7 percent lower depression risk and a 9 percent lower risk of high blood pressure, benefits tied to light, greenery, and movement rather than vitamin D synthesis. [shard_02048_72475]
Outdoor light exposure also helps regulate the circadian rhythm through pathways separate from UVB-driven vitamin D production, supporting better sleep and daytime alertness. [shard_02457_77621]

Health considerations differ meaningfully across age and sex.
Infants are uniquely vulnerable because their vitamin D stores at birth last only about a month and breast milk contains little vitamin D, so maternal deficiency directly compounds a newborn's risk. [shard_00642_73867]
A baby is typically born with only about 75 percent of its mother's vitamin D level, making prenatal sufficiency a distinct maternal-fetal priority. [shard_01540_50936]
Children and adolescents uniquely benefit from building peak bone mass, since roughly a quarter of adult bone mass accrues during just two pubertal years, while outdoor time has separately been shown to improve focus in children with ADHD. [shard_01540_50936] [shard_03248_69687]
Adult men show a distinct hormonal benefit: supplementing 3,332 IU of vitamin D daily for a year raised free testosterone by roughly 20 percent in one study. [shard_06159_64309]
Adult women carry a unique skeletal risk, since one in three women over 50 will suffer an osteoporotic fracture compared with one in five men, a gap driven largely by accelerated post-menopausal bone loss. [shard_01540_50936]
Vitamin D sufficiency has also been linked to lower body fat in women and to leaner offspring through effects on fetal metabolic programming. [shard_06159_64309]
Older adults face the clearest fall-and-fracture risk: supplementing 700-1,000 IU of vitamin D3 daily reduced falls by 19 to 26 percent, and doses above 800 IU with calcium cut fracture risk by 10 to 15 percent. [shard_02216_68326]
Adults over 40 hospitalized with COVID-19 who had sufficient vitamin D had roughly a 51 percent lower risk of severe outcomes than deficient patients, underscoring an age-related immune benefit. [shard_05622_81596]

Recommended sun exposure duration depends heavily on skin pigmentation, season, latitude, and time of day.
A light-skinned person at midday in summer typically needs only about 10 minutes of exposure on roughly 10 percent of body surface area, while darker, more melanin-rich skin needs two to three times longer for the same vitamin D yield. [shard_03119_13842]
In winter that same light-skinned person may need 30 minutes and a darker-skinned person up to 90 minutes, because a lower sun angle reduces UVB penetration. [shard_03119_13842]
A satellite-modeling study across Indian cities found clear-sky exposure for 1,000 IU ranged from about 11 to 22 minutes at midday but climbed to 85-133 minutes in northern latitudes during winter and monsoon season once cloud cover was included. [shard_06371_51490]
The optimal window for cutaneous vitamin D production is roughly 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., and exposure should stop at about one-third of the dose that would produce faint skin redness, with unprotected exposure avoided whenever the UV Index exceeds 3. [shard_03119_13842] [shard_06371_51490]

On supplementation, two consensus bodies offer complementary daily intake targets in International Units: the Institute of Medicine recommends 600 IU for ages 1-70 and 800 IU for those 71 and older, while the Endocrine Society, focused on people at risk of deficiency, suggests higher ranges of 600-1,000 IU for children and 1,500-2,000 IU for adults. [shard_02216_68326]
Tolerable upper limits also rise with age, from about 1,000 IU for young infants up to 4,000 IU for most adults, including pregnant and lactating women. [shard_00642_73867]
Vitamin D comes in two supplemental forms, plant-derived D2 (ergocalciferol) and animal-derived D3 (cholecalciferol, the form skin naturally makes), and D3 is considered clearly superior, raising and sustaining blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels roughly 87 percent more effectively than D2. [shard_00682_42272]
A controlled fortification trial found D3 raised serum vitamin D by about 75 percent over 12 weeks compared with only 33-34 percent for D2 at the same 600 IU dose, which is why most clinicians now favor D3 specifically. [shard_03061_58442]

Underexposure to sun and vitamin D carries well-documented risks, including rickets in children, osteomalacia and osteoporosis in adults, muscle weakness, higher fall and fracture rates in older adults, and greater susceptibility to respiratory infections. [shard_02216_68326] [shard_00642_73867] [shard_05622_81596]
Overexposure carries a different risk profile: UV radiation is a proven carcinogen responsible for roughly one million skin cancers and about 8,000 melanoma deaths annually in the United States, alongside accelerated skin aging. [shard_02490_38869]
True oral vitamin D toxicity is rare, generally requiring roughly 50,000 IU per day for months before hypercalcemia symptoms such as nausea, weakness, and kidney strain appear, and toxicity cannot occur from sun exposure alone because the skin self-regulates production. [shard_05608_70000] [shard_02490_38869]
Sensible mitigation bridges both risks: seek brief, unprotected midday exposure for vitamin D synthesis, then use broad-spectrum SPF 30-plus sunscreen, protective clothing, wide-brimmed hats, and shade once approaching your skin's burn threshold. [shard_03686_53028]

Checking the daily UV Index, avoiding prolonged unprotected exposure between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m., and periodically testing blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D are practical, low-cost ways to stay in the safe middle ground between deficiency and overexposure. [shard_03686_53028] [shard_02457_77621]

answer.text: As a senior research fellow at a national public health institute, I want to give the public a clear, actionable picture of what recent peer-reviewed science says about sunlight, outdoor time, and vitamin D.
The core finding is that sunlight-driven vitamin D synthesis and simply spending time outdoors deliver overlapping but distinct benefits, so both matter rather than either alone.

Our headline recommendations are brief, regular sun exposure tailored to skin tone and season, a vitamin D3 supplement in the 600-2,000 IU daily range depending on age and risk, and balancing sun exposure against skin cancer risk through shade, clothing, and timing rather than total avoidance.

Vitamin D3 is made when UVB rays convert a skin precursor into previtamin D3, which the liver and kidneys activate into the hormone governing calcium absorption, bone mineralization, and immune regulation, and this sun-made form remains active in the bloodstream roughly twice as long as vitamin D from diet or pills, so exposure and pills are not interchangeable even though both raise the same blood marker, 25-hydroxyvitamin D.
Independent of vitamin D itself, being outdoors lowers cortisol, reduces blood pressure, improves mood, and increases physical activity, effects that persist even when vitamin D status is unchanged.

One analysis found roughly 30 minutes outdoors was linked to about a 7 percent lower depression risk and a 9 percent lower risk of high blood pressure, benefits tied to light, greenery, and movement rather than vitamin D synthesis.
Outdoor light also helps regulate the circadian rhythm and boosts alertness through pathways separate from UVB-driven vitamin D production.
Health considerations differ meaningfully across age and sex, and each group carries at least one distinct benefit or risk.
Infants are uniquely vulnerable because their vitamin D stores at birth last only about a month and breast milk contains little vitamin D, so maternal deficiency directly compounds a newborn's risk.
A baby is typically born with only about 75 percent of its mother's vitamin D level, making prenatal sufficiency a distinct priority for pregnant women.

Children and adolescents uniquely benefit from building peak bone mass, since roughly a quarter of adult bone mass accrues during just two pubertal years, while outdoor time separately improves focus in children with ADHD.
Adult men show a distinct hormonal benefit: supplementing 3,332 IU of vitamin D daily for a year raised free testosterone by roughly 20 percent in one study.

Adult women carry a unique skeletal risk, since one in three women over 50 will suffer an osteoporotic fracture compared with one in five men, a gap driven largely by accelerated post-menopausal bone loss.

Older adults face the clearest fall-and-fracture risk: supplementing 700-1,000 IU of vitamin D3 daily reduced falls by 19 to 26 percent, and doses above 800 IU with calcium cut fracture risk by 10 to 15 percent.

Older adults also gain a distinct immune benefit, since low vitamin D has been linked to a 64 percent higher risk of community-acquired pneumonia, prompting Irish researchers to recommend supplementation specifically for adults over 50.
Recommended sun exposure duration depends heavily on skin pigmentation, season, latitude, and time of day.

A light-skinned person at midday in summer typically needs only about 10 minutes of exposure on roughly 10 percent of body surface area, while darker, more melanin-rich skin needs two to three times longer for the same vitamin D yield.
In winter that same light-skinned person may need 30 minutes and a darker-skinned person up to 90 minutes, because a lower sun angle reduces UVB penetration.

A satellite-modeling study across Indian cities found clear-sky exposure for 1,000 IU ranged from about 11 to 22 minutes at midday but climbed to 85-133 minutes in northern latitudes during winter and monsoon season once cloud cover was included.

The optimal window for cutaneous vitamin D production is roughly 11 a.m. to 2 p.m., exposure should stop at about one-third of the dose that would produce faint skin redness, and unprotected exposure should be avoided whenever the UV Index reaches 3 or above.

On supplementation, two consensus bodies offer complementary daily intake targets in International Units: the Institute of Medicine recommends 600 IU for ages 1-70 and 800 IU for those 71 and older, while the Endocrine Society, focused on people at risk of deficiency, suggests higher ranges of 600-1,000 IU for children and 1,500-2,000 IU for adults.
Tolerable upper limits also rise with age, from about 1,000 IU for young infants up to 4,000 IU for most adults, including pregnant and lactating women.

Vitamin D comes in two supplemental forms, plant-derived D2 (ergocalciferol) and animal-derived D3 (cholecalciferol, the form skin naturally makes), and D3 is considered clearly superior, raising and sustaining blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels roughly 87 percent more effectively than D2.

A controlled fortification trial found D3 raised serum vitamin D by about 75 percent over 12 weeks compared with only 33-34 percent for D2 at the same 600 IU dose, which is why clinicians now favor D3 specifically.

Underexposure carries well-documented risks, including rickets in children, osteomalacia and osteoporosis in adults, muscle weakness, higher fall and fracture rates in older adults, and greater susceptibility to respiratory infections.

Overexposure carries a different risk profile: UV radiation is a proven carcinogen responsible for roughly one million skin cancers and about 8,000 melanoma deaths annually in the United States, alongside accelerated skin aging.

True oral vitamin D toxicity is rare, generally requiring roughly 50,000 IU per day for months before hypercalcemia symptoms such as nausea, weakness, and kidney strain appear, and toxicity cannot occur from sun exposure alone because skin self-regulates production.

Sensible mitigation bridges both risks: seek brief, unprotected midday exposure for vitamin D synthesis, then use broad-spectrum SPF 30-plus sunscreen, protective clothing, a wide-brimmed hat, and shade once approaching your skin's burn threshold.
People with photosensitizing conditions such as lupus, or on certain sun-sensitizing medications, may need stricter shade-and-clothing-first strategies instead of deliberate sun exposure.
Checking the daily UV Index and periodically testing blood 25-hydroxyvitamin D remain the simplest ways to stay in the safe middle ground between deficiency and overexposure.
